report:
**Conclusion: no.** Current evidence does not support coenzyme Q10 (CoQ10) as improving Parkinson’s movement symptoms or slowing motor disability.

Why the idea arose: a small early randomized trial in untreated, early Parkinson’s found a statistically significant difference in worsening of the total UPDRS disability score for 1,200 mg/day versus placebo (P=.04), with a dose-response *trend* (P=.09). But this was a preliminary signal, not proof, and the authors said a larger confirmatory trial was needed.  
https://jamanetwork.com/journals/jamaneurology/fullarticle/782965

That confirmation did not materialize. The much larger NIH/Parkinson Study Group QE3 trial of high-dose CoQ10 in early Parkinson’s was stopped after an interim analysis found no improvement versus placebo. The trial specifically tested whether CoQ10 could slow clinical decline.  
https://clinicaltrials.gov/study/NCT00740714  
https://www.parkinson.org/living-with-parkinsons/treatment/over-the-counter-complementary-therapies

A 2022 systematic review notes biological rationale—mitochondrial dysfunction/oxidative stress and altered CoQ10 measures in some Parkinsonian tissues—but therapeutic-trial evidence has been inconsistent and has not established clinical efficacy. Biological plausibility or low measured levels does not show that supplementation improves movement.  
https://www.mdpi.com/2075-4426/12/6/975

CoQ10 appears generally well tolerated at studied doses, but it should not replace evidence-based Parkinson’s treatments. It can interact with blood thinners/aspirin and may affect blood pressure; discuss it with the prescribing clinician, particularly if taking anticoagulants.
